## Key terms

{{< glossary computing-system hardware software von-neumann cpu memory storage instruction-cycle abstraction-level isa compiler digital-platform >}}

## 1.1 What a computing system is

A **computing system** combines hardware, software and data to perform four
functions: **input**, **processing**, **storage** and **output**. Almost every
computer follows the **stored-program (von Neumann) model**: the program is
kept in memory like data. Its parts are the **CPU** (control unit, **ALU**,
registers), the **main memory** (RAM: fast, volatile), the **I/O devices**
including **storage** (flash: permanent), and the **bus** that connects them.
The CPU repeats the **instruction cycle** — fetch, decode, execute — billions
of times per second (3 GHz = 3 × 10^9^ ticks per second).

![The stored-program (von Neumann) model.](images/von-neumann.png){width=82%}

![The instruction cycle.](images/instruction-cycle.png){width=56%}

{{< sim file="sims/one-frame.html" poster="sims/one-frame.png" title="Tap Runner: inside one frame" kind="game" height="600" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Inside the computer"}
Choose the right term or value.

::: {.match extra="registers|500 million"}
The part of the CPU that performs arithmetic and comparisons.
:   the ALU

The memory that loses its contents when the power is off.
:   RAM

The three steps that the CPU repeats for every instruction.
:   fetch, decode, execute

The clock ticks available per frame for a 3 GHz core at 60 fps.
:   50 million

:   storage

:   the stored-program model

## 1.2 The computer as a multilevel machine

A processor understands only its machine language. Computers are therefore
built as a stack of **levels of abstraction**, each with a more convenient
language implemented by the level below: 0 digital logic, 1 microarchitecture,
2 **instruction set architecture (ISA)**, 3 operating system machine,
4 assembly language, 5 problem-oriented languages such as C#. A program moves
down by **translation** (a **compiler** converts it before it runs) or
**interpretation** (an **interpreter** executes it step by step). Phones use
the **ARM** ISA, PCs and the PlayStation and Xbox use **x86-64**: the same C#
game is translated for each.

![The levels a game passes through.](images/levels.png){width=72%}

![One C# game, translated for ARM and for x86-64.](images/build-targets.png){width=86%}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Levels and languages"}
Choose the right level, program or ISA.

::: {.match extra="digital logic"}
The level at which hardware and software meet.
:   the ISA

The level that provides files, processes and memory management.
:   operating system machine

The program that converts a whole program before it runs.
:   compiler

The program that carries out another program instruction by instruction.
:   interpreter

The ISA of almost all smartphones.
:   ARM

The ISA of desktop PCs and of the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series.
:   x86-64
:::
:::

## 1.3 Classes of computing systems

Games run on five classes of computers: **embedded** systems (controllers,
toys), **mobile** devices (phones, tablets: battery, no fan), **personal
computers**, **consoles** (fixed hardware tuned for games) and **servers** in
data centres (online play, cloud gaming). They differ mainly in how much they
compute and at what energy cost. Performance has grown for decades with
**Moore's law**: the number of transistors per chip doubling about every two
years.

![Five classes of computers.](images/computer-classes.png){width=94%}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Which class?"}
Choose the class of computer, or the law.

::: {.match extra="personal computer"}
It reads the buttons inside a game controller.
:   embedded

It runs the online matches of thousands of players.
:   server

Fixed hardware designed and tuned for games.
:   console

Battery-powered, no fan, the largest gaming platform.
:   mobile

Transistor counts double about every two years.
:   Moore's law
:::
:::

## 1.4 Digital platforms in the games industry

A **digital platform** is a hardware family + an operating system + an SDK +
a distribution channel with its own rules: Android with Google Play, iOS with
the App Store, Windows with Steam, the consoles with their makers' stores, and
cloud gaming. The platform owner sets the rules and may **certify** each game
before release. Studios use **cross-platform** engines, but still face
**fragmentation**: thousands of Android models with different screens,
processors and versions.

![The four layers of a platform.](images/platform-stack.png){width=56%}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Platforms"}
Choose the right term.

::: {.match extra="App Store"}
Hardware + operating system + SDK + a store with rules.
:   digital platform

The main store of the Android platform.
:   Google Play

An engine that builds one game for several platforms.
:   cross-platform

Thousands of Android models with different screens and system versions.
:   fragmentation

The approval process of a console maker before a game is released.
:   certification
:::
:::

## Game challenge: Tap Runner {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

**Tap Runner** is an endless runner: the character runs by itself and the
player taps to jump over blocks. The game targets 60 fps and saves the best
distance. It is released on Android phones, on iPhones and on Windows PCs;
the phone used for testing has a 2.4 GHz CPU core.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Tap Runner on three platforms (harder)"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="RAM|ARM"}
The input device used to jump in the phone version.
:   touch screen

Where the best distance is kept while the phone is switched off.
:   storage

The clock ticks per frame for the test phone's core at 60 fps.
:   40 million

The ISA for which the Windows build is generated.
:   x86-64

The level that differs between the iPhone build and the Windows build.
:   the ISA

The level at which the game's rules are written.
:   problem-oriented language
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- Computing system: hardware + software + data; input, processing, storage, output.
- Stored-program model: CPU, RAM, I/O and storage on a bus; fetch–decode–execute.
- Memory (RAM) is fast and volatile; storage is permanent.
- A computer is a multilevel machine; programs reach the hardware by translation or interpretation; the ISA is the boundary.
- Five classes: embedded, mobile, personal, console, server.
- A platform = hardware + OS + SDK + store and rules; engines are cross-platform, devices are fragmented.
